etymology: From flower (Old French flour, Latin flos) + child. Coined in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury in 1966–67 for the young hippies who carried and handed out flowers as emblems of peace, the outgrowth of Allen Ginsberg’s 1965 essay urging “flower power” protest (Online Etymology Dictionary dates flower child to 1967). By the Summer of Love the press used it for the whole gentle, barefoot, daisy-in-the-rifle-barrel wing of the counterculture.
biblical_def: A flower child was the gentlest face of the 1960s counterculture: a young person, usually a runaway or a dropout, who wore flowers in the hair, preached peace and love, refused the business suit and the draft card, and believed that innocence and goodwill could remake the world. Your grandparents remember them on the evening news and on the album covers. The Christian observation is twofold. First, the longing was not wicked. Gentleness is a fruit of the Spirit, and the Lord Jesus sent His disciples out "harmless as doves" (Mat 10:16). Second, the flower was a truer emblem than its wearers knew. Scripture uses the flower again and again as the picture of what fades: "all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass" (1Pe 1:24). The flower children hoped to build a new age on youth, feeling, and good intentions, and within a few years the Haight was a slum of hard drugs and broken runaways. What does not fade is not the flower but the Word: "The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever" (Isa 40:8). A grandparent can tell a grandchild honestly: we wanted peace and we were right to want it; we looked for it in the wrong garden. The Prince of Peace is the only ground in which gentleness takes root and lasts.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (1967) for a gentle, flower-carrying hippie idealist — a longing for peace planted in youth and feeling, which Scripture calls the flower that fadeth beside the Word that stands for ever.
webster_full: FLOWER CHILD, n. (Boomer slang, 1967; pl. flower children) A young hippie of the gentle, pacifist sort, who carried or wore flowers as tokens of peace and love; by extension any naive, peace-loving idealist. "She was a real flower child in ’67."

Webster (1828) — FLOWER, noun [Latin flos, floris, a flower; floreo, to blossom. See Flourish .] 1. In botany, that part of a plant which contains the organs of fructification, with their coverings. A flower when complete, consists of a calyx, corol, stamen and pistil; but the essential parts are the anther and stigma, which are sufficient to constitute a flower either together in hermaphrodite flowers, or separate in male and female flowers. 2. In vulgar acceptation, a blossom or flower is the flower bud of a plant, when the petals are expanded; open petals being considered as the principal thing in constituting a flower But in botany, the petals are now considered as a finer sort of covering, and not at all necessary to constitute a flower 3. The early part of life, or rather of manhood; the prime; youthful vigor; youth; as the flower of age or of life. 4.
Decode for families: when a grandparent says "I was a flower child," he or she usually means "I believed love would fix the world" — ask what happened to that belief, and listen.
scriptures: Isa 40:8
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever.
For all flesh is as grass, and all the glory of man as the flower of grass. The grass withereth, and the flower thereof falleth away:
Behold, I send you forth as sheep in the midst of wolves: be ye therefore wise as serpents, and harmless as doves.
Mat 6:28
And why take ye thought for raiment? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin:
Jas 1:11

For the sun is no sooner risen with a burning heat, but it withereth the grass, and the flower thereof falleth, and the grace of the fashion of it perisheth: so also shall the rich man fade away in his ways.
corruption_summary: The flower child sought peace in youth, innocence, and feeling; Scripture names the flower as the very picture of what fades and plants peace only in the Word that stands for ever.
corruption_paragraphs: The movement’s error was not its gentleness but its anthropology. It assumed the human heart is a garden that only needs to be left alone to bloom — that if war, money, and parents were taken away, love would grow on its own. Scripture says the opposite: the heart is the source of the fightings, not their victim. The Haight-Ashbury proved it inside of two summers. The same streets that handed out daisies in 1967 were by 1968 full of runaways, speed, and exploitation, and the gentlest of the flower children were the first to be devoured. Innocence without the fear of the LORD is not protected; it is merely unarmed.

Yet the Lord Jesus also pointed to flowers. "Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow; they toil not, neither do they spin" (Mat 6:28) — and the lesson He drew was trust in the Father who clothes them, not a life of drifting. The Christian answer to the flower child is not the cynic but the dove who walks among wolves with a wise head (Mat 10:16), whose peace is not a mood but a Person, and whose bloom is rooted where the sun cannot wither it (Jas 1:11).
roots_summary: Latin flos → Old French flour → English flower; 1965 "flower power" (Ginsberg) → 1967 flower child / flower children, Haight-Ashbury.
roots_lines: Latin flos, floris — a blossom; figuratively the prime or best part of a thing
Old French flour → Middle English flour — blossom; also the finest part of grain (hence flour)
1965: Allen Ginsberg’s essay "How to Make a March/Spectacle" urges protesters to carry flowers — "flower power"
1967: flower child / flower children in the San Francisco press during the Summer of Love
Scripture: the flower of the field as the emblem of what fades (Isa 40:8; 1Pe 1:24; Jas 1:11)
usage: "Grandma swears she was a flower child before she met Grandpa at the Baptist picnic."
The flower child sought peace in innocence; the Christian finds it in the Word that stands for ever (Isa 40:8).
Be harmless as a dove, but not witless — the Lord sent His doves among wolves with wise heads (Mat 10:16).

etymology: Two older pieces joined in the 1960s. The Man is African-American and jazz slang from the early twentieth century for a white boss, the police, or any authority holding the whip; to stick it to (someone) — to treat harshly, to take advantage of, to punish — is American slang current by the mid-twentieth century. Joined, stick it to the Man became a counterculture and anti-war rallying phrase in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and was revived for a new generation by the 2003 film School of Rock.
biblical_def: To stick it to the Man is to defy authority — the boss, the school, the police, the government, the whole adult order — and to enjoy doing it. It is the Boomer generation’s anthem of rebellion, and its grandchildren still sing it. The Christian observation: Scripture knows two very different things that can wear this slogan. One is righteous refusal. When the rulers commanded the apostles to stop preaching, "Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men" (Act 5:29). Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego would not bow, and Daniel kept his window open toward Jerusalem. That is not sticking it to the Man; it is obeying a higher Master at the cost of one’s neck. The other is plain rebellion, the reflex that treats every authority as an enemy because it is an authority. Against that, the apostle writes: "Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God" (Rom 13:1). The Christian is told to "Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king" (1Pe 2:17) — and that was written under Nero. The test a father can teach is simple: am I refusing a command because it requires me to sin, or because I do not like being commanded? The first may be faithfulness. The second is the oldest sin in the garden.
webster_summary: Boomer counterculture phrase (late 1960s) for defying authority with relish — a slogan Scripture divides into righteous refusal (Act 5:29) and plain rebellion (Rom 13:1).
webster_full: STICK IT TO THE MAN, phr. (Boomer slang, late 1960s–70s; revived 2003) To defy, frustrate, or get the better of those in authority — employer, government, police, school — especially by an act of open rebellion. "Quit the job and stick it to the Man."
The Man — authority personified; the boss, the police, the establishment (see The Man).
Stick it to — to treat harshly; to impose upon; to get revenge on.
Decode for families: the phrase assumes authority is the villain of every story. Scripture assumes authority is God’s servant (Rom 13:4) — often a bad one, but never ours to despise.
scriptures: Rom 13:1
Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
Honour all men. Love the brotherhood. Fear God. Honour the king.
Tit 3:1
Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,
My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change:
corruption_summary: The slogan baptizes every defiance as heroism; Scripture honors refusal only where obedience to men would mean disobedience to God, and calls the rest rebellion.
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase flatters the rebel. It casts him as the little guy, the truth-teller, the free man, and casts every authority as the villain. Some authorities have earned that — the 1960s had real injustice to resist, and the believer is not commanded to call evil good. But the slogan does not discriminate. It trains a young man to feel a thrill whenever he defies, and to read every rule as an insult. That is not courage; it is the posture of the first rebellion, which also said, in effect, "Yea, hath God said?" Proverbs is blunt about the company it keeps: "My son, fear thou the LORD and the king: and meddle not with them that are given to change" (Pro 24:21).

The Christian alternative is not servility. The apostles stood before the council and refused (Act 5:29), the midwives disobeyed Pharaoh, Daniel defied a decree. But in every case the refusal was narrow, open, respectful, and willing to bear the penalty. They did not stick it to the Man; they honored the king while declining to sin for him (1Pe 2:17). Paul tells Titus to keep believers "subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work" (Tit 3:1). The Christian is the freest man in the room precisely because he is not ruled by his resentment.
roots_summary: Early 20th-c. AAVE / jazz the Man (authority) + mid-20th-c. American stick it to (treat harshly) → late-1960s counterculture slogan → 2003 revival (School of Rock).
roots_lines: The Man — early 20th-c. African-American and jazz slang for the white boss, the police, the authority in charge
Stick it to — mid-20th-c. American slang: to treat harshly, to overcharge, to take revenge
Late 1960s–early 1970s: joined as a counterculture and anti-war slogan
2003: revived for Millennials by the film School of Rock
Scripture: Rom 13:1 (the powers ordained of God) beside Act 5:29 (obey God rather than men)
usage: "Grandpa says he burned his draft card to stick it to the Man; Grandma says he was mostly showing off."
Refuse the sin, not the ruler: "We ought to obey God rather than men" (Act 5:29).
Honour the king even when you must decline his order (1Pe 2:17).

etymology: From establish (Old French establir, Latin stabilire, "to make firm"). For centuries the establishment meant a state church — the Church of England "by law established." The modern sense of an entrenched ruling class was popularized by the British journalist Henry Fairlie in The Spectator (September 1955), writing of the network of officials and families who really ran Britain. American students imported it in the early 1960s, and by 1967 "the Establishment" was the counterculture’s name for every grown-up institution at once: government, business, university, church, and parents.
biblical_def: To a Boomer of 1968, the Establishment was the whole interlocking order of power — Washington, Wall Street, the Pentagon, the dean’s office, the denomination, and Dad — that seemed to decide everything and answer to no one. The young set themselves against it, and many of them later ran it. The Christian observation begins where Scripture begins: there is an establishment, and it is God’s. "He removeth kings, and setteth up kings" (Dan 2:21); every earthly order stands only so long as He establishes it. So the believer neither worships the human establishment nor despises it. He does not worship it, because "Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help" (Psa 146:3), and because the establishments of the world have often "set themselves" and taken "counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed" (Psa 2:2) — that is how the Lord of glory was crucified, by priests and governors acting together. He does not despise it, because the same God commands honor to the powers that be (Rom 13:1). And he knows how the story ends: "He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh" (Psa 2:4). The Church herself is God’s establishment in the world, built on the one foundation that no protest can shake and no committee can replace.
webster_summary: Boomer counterculture name (from 1955 British usage) for the entrenched ruling order — government, business, university, church — which Scripture neither worships (Psa 146:3) nor despises (Rom 13:1), because God removeth and setteth up kings.
webster_full: THE ESTABLISHMENT, n. (Boomer slang, 1960s; from British political usage, 1955) The dominant group of officials, institutions, and families who hold power in a society and resist change; the "system." "Don’t sell out to the Establishment."

Webster (1828) — ESTABLISHMENT, noun The act of establishing, founding, ratifying or ordaining. 1. Settlement; ; fixed state. 2. Confirmation; ratification of what has been settled or made. 3. Settled regulation; form; ordinance; system of laws; constitution of government. Bring in that establishment by which all men should be contained in duty. 4. Fixed or stated allowance for subsistence; income; salary. His excellency--might gradually lessen your establishment 5. That which is fixed or established; as a permanent military force, a fixed garrison, a local government, an agency, a factory, etc. The king has establishments to support, in the four quarters of the globe.
Older English sense: the Establishment — a church established by law, as the Church of England.
Decode for families: the Boomers who rebelled against the Establishment became it. Every generation must learn that the problem is not who sits in the chair but what sits in the heart.
scriptures: Dan 2:21
And he changeth the times and the seasons: he removeth kings, and setteth up kings: he giveth wisdom unto the wise, and knowledge to them that know understanding:
Psa 2:2
The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD, and against his anointed, saying,
Psa 2:4
He that sitteth in the heavens shall laugh: the Lord shall have them in derision.
Put not your trust in princes, nor in the son of man, in whom there is no help.
But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;
corruption_summary: The counterculture made the Establishment the enemy and youth the savior; Scripture teaches that God sets up and removes every establishment, and that trust in princes — old or young — is misplaced.
corruption_paragraphs: The word did two things at once. It named something real: there are networks of power, and they do protect themselves, and the Psalmist saw the kings and rulers of the earth take counsel together against the LORD (Psa 2:2). But it also built a myth: that the Establishment is the source of evil and that the young, the outsiders, and the protesters are innocent of it. History closed that myth quickly. The students who occupied the dean’s office in 1968 held the dean’s office by 1998. Power did not become pure by changing hands; it changed hands and stayed the same. "Put not your trust in princes" (Psa 146:3) includes the princes you elected yourself.

God’s way of overturning establishments is not the protest but the cross. "God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty" (1Co 1:27). A carpenter’s Son, executed by the establishment of His day, rose and outlasted Rome. The Christian therefore holds every human institution loosely, honors it duly, prays for it faithfully, and laughs with the One who sits in the heavens (Psa 2:4).
roots_summary: Latin stabilire → Old French establir → English establish; 17th-c. "the Establishment" = state church → 1955 Fairlie (ruling class) → 1960s US counterculture.
roots_lines: Latin stabilis — firm, steadfast; stabilire — to make firm
Old French establir → Middle English establisshen — to set up, to settle
17th–19th c.: the Establishment — the church established by law (Church of England)
1955: Henry Fairlie, The Spectator — the informal ruling class of Britain
1960s: US counterculture — government, business, university, church, and parents together
usage: "In ’68 your grandfather was against the Establishment; by ’88 he was on the bank board."
God removeth kings and setteth up kings (Dan 2:21); no establishment stands without Him.
Honor the powers, but put not your trust in princes (Psa 146:3).

etymology: Peace + the Yiddish/Russian suffix -nik (one who is connected with something), which entered American English with Sputnik (1957) and beatnik (coined by San Francisco columnist Herb Caen, 1958). Peacenik appears by 1963 as a mildly mocking name for anti-war and anti-nuclear demonstrators, and became common during the Vietnam protests. Opponents used it as a jab; many protesters wore it as a badge.
biblical_def: A peacenik was an anti-war activist of the 1960s and 70s — marching against the bomb, against Vietnam, against the draft — usually said with a smirk by those who thought him naive or disloyal. The Christian observation: the word mocks something the Lord Jesus blessed, and it also exposes something the movement lacked. Our Lord said, "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Mat 5:9). The believer is commanded, "If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men" (Rom 12:18), and Isaiah’s vision of swords beaten into plowshares (Isa 2:4) is engraved on the wall of the United Nations because it is the deepest hope of every honest heart. So a Christian ought never to sneer at the longing for peace. But Scripture is not pacifist in the way many peaceniks were. It knows "a time of war, and a time of peace" (Ecc 3:8); it gives the magistrate the sword; and it warns against the prophets who cry "Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14). Isaiah’s plowshares come only when the LORD Himself shall "judge among the nations" (Isa 2:4). The peacemaker Christ blessed is not the one who refuses every conflict but the one who brings men to the reconciliation His blood purchased — first with God, then with one another.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (by 1963) for an anti-war activist, often derisive — a longing Christ blessed in the peacemakers (Mat 5:9), but which Scripture roots in reconciliation with God, not the mere absence of war.
webster_full: PEACENIK, n. (Boomer slang, by 1963; often derisive) An anti-war or anti-nuclear activist; a pacifist demonstrator. "A bunch of peaceniks were picketing the recruiting office."

Webster (1828) — PEACE, noun [Latin pax, paco, to appease.] 1. In a general sense, a state of quiet or tranquillity; freedom from disturbance or agitation; applicable to society, to individuals, or to the temper of the mind. 2. Freedom from war with a foreign nation; public quiet. 3. Freedom from internal commotion or civil war. 4. Freedom from private quarrels, suits or disturbance.
Formed on the pattern of beatnik (1958) and Sputnik (1957); compare refusenik, no-goodnik.
Decode for families: the word was a sneer. The Christian may disagree with a protester’s politics without sneering at his desire for peace.
scriptures: Mat 5:9
Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.
If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.
Isa 2:4

And he shall judge among the nations, and shall rebuke many people: and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.
Ecc 3:8
A time to love, and a time to hate; a time of war, and a time of peace.
Jer 6:14
They have healed also the hurt of the daughter of my people slightly, saying, Peace, peace; when there is no peace.
corruption_summary: The word mocked the longing for peace, and the movement often made peace an end in itself; Scripture blesses peacemakers but grounds peace in the judgment and reconciliation of God, not in disarmament alone.
corruption_paragraphs: There are two corruptions here, one on each side of the picket line. The first belongs to the mockers. They made a joke of a hope the prophets held sacred, and in doing so they implied that the desire for peace is weakness. Our Lord blessed it (Mat 5:9). A Christian father should teach his son to honor the desire even when he disputes the policy.

The second belongs to the movement itself. Much of the peace movement believed that peace is simply the absence of war, achievable by marching and disarmament, and that the warrior is always the villain. Scripture knows better. There is "a time of war, and a time of peace" (Ecc 3:8), and the false prophets of Jeremiah’s day were precisely the ones who cried "Peace, peace" when judgment was at the gate (Jer 6:14). The plowshares of Isaiah 2:4 are the fruit of the LORD’s own judging and rebuking of the nations. Peace is not the first thing; it is the fruit of righteousness. The true peacemaker carries the gospel of the One who "made peace through the blood of his cross" — and that peace, once made with God, goes on to make peace between men.
roots_summary: Old French pais, Latin pax → English peace + Yiddish / Slavic -nik (via Sputnik 1957, beatnik 1958) → peacenik, by 1963.
roots_lines: Latin pax, pacis — a compact, an agreement, peace
Hebrew shalom — wholeness, well-being, peace with God and man
Yiddish / Slavic agent suffix -nik — one associated with a thing
1957–58: Sputnik, beatnik popularize -nik in American slang
By 1963: peacenik, often derisive, for anti-war and anti-nuclear demonstrators
usage: "Uncle Ray called them peaceniks; Aunt Carol marched with them."
Blessed are the peacemakers (Mat 5:9) — but peace with God comes before peace on the picket line.
Beware the cry of "Peace, peace; when there is no peace" (Jer 6:14).

etymology: The anti-Vietnam War slogan of the mid-1960s, printed on buttons, posters, and placards by 1965–67. The folklorist Gershon Legman claimed to have coined it in a 1963 lecture at Ohio University; whatever its first speaker, its power lay in pairing the sexual revolution with the peace movement in four words. It was everywhere at the 1967 Summer of Love and remained the defining slogan of the era.
biblical_def: Make love, not war was the counterculture’s whole creed on a button: the war in Vietnam was the work of repressed, uptight old men, and the cure was free sexual love among the young. The Christian observation: the slogan uses the holiest word in the language to mean its cheapest counterfeit, and it gets the source of war exactly backwards. James asks the question the slogan thought it had answered: "From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (Jas 4:1). War does not come from too little appetite; it comes from appetite unruled. The free love of the 1960s did not end the fighting; it moved the battlefield into the home, and the children of broken marriages inherited the casualties. Scripture’s love is another thing entirely. "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up" (1Co 13:4). Its highest act is not a night but a death: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends" (Joh 15:13). And God’s will for the body is plain: "For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication" (1Th 4:3). The Christian does not answer the slogan with "make war"; he answers with the love that keeps covenant — the only love that has ever brought peace into a house.
webster_summary: The mid-1960s anti-war slogan pairing the peace movement with the sexual revolution — a creed Scripture overturns, since wars come from lusts (Jas 4:1) and true love lays down its life (Joh 15:13).
webster_full: MAKE LOVE, NOT WAR, slogan (Boomer era, c. 1965–67) The anti-Vietnam War motto of the counterculture, urging sexual freedom and pacifism in place of militarism. Printed on buttons and placards; chanted at demonstrations.

Webster (1828) — LOVE, noun 1. An affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth of any kind, or by the qualities of an object which communicate pleasure, sensual or intellectual. It is opposed to hatred. love between the sexes, is a compound affection, consisting of esteem, benevolence, and animal desire. love is excited by pleasing qualities of any kind, as by kindness, benevolence, charity, and by the qualities which render social intercourse agreeable. In the latter case, love is ardent friendship, or a strong attachment springing from good will and esteem, and the pleasure derived from the company, civilities and kindness of others. Between certain natural relatives, love seems to be in some cases instinctive. Such is the love of a mother for her child, which manifests itself toward an infant, before any particular qualities in the child are unfolded.

Webster (1828) — WAR, noun [G., to perplex, embroil, disturb. The primary sense of the root is to strive, struggle, urge, drive, or to turn, to twist.] 1. A contest between nations or states, carried on by force, either for defense, or for revenging insults and redressing wrongs, for the extension of commerce or acquisition of territory, or for obtaining and establishing the superiority and dominion of one over the other. These objects are accomplished by the slaughter or capture of troops, and the capture and destruction of ships, towns and property. Among rude nations, war is often waged and carried on for plunder. As war is the contest of nations or states, it always implies that such contest is authorized by the monarch or the sovereign power of the nation. When war is commenced by attacking a nation in peace, it si called an offensive war and such attack is aggressive.
Decode for families: make love here does not mean what your great-grandmother meant by it (to court, to woo). The slogan is the sexual revolution in four words.
scriptures: Jas 4:1
From whence come wars and fightings among you? come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?
Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up,
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
For this is the will of God, even your sanctification, that ye should abstain from fornication:
Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
corruption_summary: The slogan names lust as love and repression as the cause of war; Scripture names lust as the cause of war (Jas 4:1) and covenant self-giving as love.
corruption_paragraphs: Notice what happens to the word love. In 1828 to make love meant to court a woman with a view to marriage. By 1967 it meant sexual intercourse with anyone, anywhere, without covenant. The slogan finished the theft: it took the word for the highest thing and pinned it to the appetite, then offered the appetite as the remedy for violence. But appetite is the root of violence. "Come they not hence, even of your lusts that war in your members?" (Jas 4:1). The generation that was told to make love instead of war got both — the war in Southeast Asia and a second war fought in family courts for the next fifty years.

Paul has the true pairing. "Ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another" (Gal 5:13). Liberty for the flesh is the slogan; liberty for service is the gospel. A father tells his son: the strongest man in the room is not the one who takes what he wants but the one who lays down his life for his friends (Joh 15:13) — and for his wife, and for his children. That love ends wars.
roots_summary: Old English lufu (love) + Old English werre / Old French werre (war); make love = to court (17th–19th c.) → to have sex (20th c.) → mid-1960s anti-war slogan.
roots_lines: Old English lufu — love, affection; Greek agapē (Joh 15:13) — self-giving love
Late Old English werre, from Old North French werre (Frankish werra, confusion, strife)
17th–19th c.: to make love — to pay court, to woo
20th c.: to make love — to have sexual intercourse
c. 1965–67: Make love, not war on anti-Vietnam buttons and placards
usage: "Grandpa still has the button: MAKE LOVE NOT WAR. Grandma made him put it in a drawer."
Wars come from lusts that war in our members (Jas 4:1); the slogan prescribed the disease as the cure.
Greater love hath no man than this (Joh 15:13) — love that dies for its friends, not love that uses them.

etymology: A radical slogan of the late 1960s associated above all with the Black Panther Party (founded Oakland, 1966), whose rallies chanted "All power to the people" by 1968–69; it was adopted across the student and anti-war left, and John Lennon released the single "Power to the People" in March 1971. The raised fist usually went with it.
biblical_def: Power to the people was the cry of the late-1960s radical left: take power away from the government, the corporations, and the police, and hand it to ordinary people — usually through street protest, sometimes through revolution. The Christian observation: the slogan asks the right question, "Who has power?" and gives the wrong answer. Scripture’s answer is the first and last word on the matter: "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God" (Psa 62:11). Our Lord told Pilate, the most powerful man in Judaea, "Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above" (Joh 19:11). Power is never the people’s by nature, nor the king’s; it is God’s, lent to men as stewards and answerable to Him. Scripture also shows what happens when power is simply handed to the people with no fear of God above them: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Jdg 21:25), and the book of Judges ends in civil war and atrocity. Yet there is a power God does give to ordinary people, and freely: "as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God" (Joh 1:12), and "ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you" (Act 1:8). That is the only power to the people that ever turned the world upside down without a single gun.
webster_summary: Late-1960s radical slogan (Black Panthers; Lennon, 1971) demanding that power pass to ordinary people — answered by Scripture: power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11), who gives sinners power to become His sons (Joh 1:12).
webster_full: POWER TO THE PEOPLE, slogan (Boomer era, late 1960s; Black Panther Party; John Lennon single, 1971) A demand that political and economic power be transferred from elites and institutions to ordinary citizens; often accompanied by a raised fist.

Webster (1828) — POWER, noun [The Latin has posse, possum, potes, potentia. The primary sense of the verb is to strain, to exert force.] 1. In a philosophical sense, the faculty of doing or performing any thing; the faculty of moving or of producing a change in something; ability or strength. A man raises his hand by his own power or by power moves another body. The exertion of power proceeds from the will, and in strictness, no being destitute of will or intelligence, can exert power power in man is active or speculative. Active power is that which moves the body; speculative power is that by which we see, judge, remember, or in general, by which we think. Power may exist without exertion. We have power to speak when we are silent. Power has been distinguished also into active and passive, the power of doing or moving, and the power of receiving impressions or of suffering.
Decode for families: the slogan is a theology of power with God left out. Ask your children, "Whose is the power?" and teach them Psalm 62:11.
scriptures: God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God.
Jesus answered, Thou couldest have no power at all against me, except it were given thee from above: therefore he that delivered me unto thee hath the greater sin.
In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.
Joh 1:12
But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name:
Act 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
corruption_summary: The slogan relocates sovereignty from God to the crowd; Scripture places all power in God, warns of every man doing right in his own eyes, and gives the people a better power — to become sons of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Every revolutionary slogan is a creed about where power comes from. The divine right of kings said it came from God to the king, and stopped there. Power to the people said it rises from the crowd, and stops there. Both are idolatries of a sort. The Reformed tradition, from Calvin through Rutherford’s Lex, Rex, held that power is God’s alone, delegated to magistrates under His law and answerable to Him, and that lesser magistrates may resist tyranny lawfully. That is very different from the street’s version, in which the crowd simply becomes the new king — and crowds have shouted both "Hosanna" and "Crucify him" in the same week.

Judges shows the end of the road: "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Jdg 21:25), and the people’s power produced the Levite’s concubine and the near-destruction of Benjamin. The gospel offers a different transfer of power. It does not take power from God and give it to man; it takes rebels and gives them power to become sons of God (Joh 1:12), and then sends them out with the power of the Holy Ghost (Act 1:8). Twelve unarmed men with that power did more to the Roman establishment than every raised fist of 1968.
roots_summary: Latin posse → Old French poeir → English power; Latin populus → people; late-1960s Black Panther chant → 1971 Lennon single.
roots_lines: Latin posse, potere — to be able → Old French poeir → English power
Latin populus → Old French pueple → English people
Greek exousia — authority, delegated right (Joh 1:12; Joh 19:11)
1966–69: Black Panther Party rallies — "All power to the people"
1971: John Lennon’s single "Power to the People"
usage: "Grandpa raised his fist and said ‘power to the people’ just to annoy Dad at Thanksgiving."
Power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11) — not to the king, not to the crowd.
The gospel’s power to the people: power to become the sons of God (Joh 1:12).

etymology: From sit + in, on the pattern of the labor sit-down strike of the 1930s (the Flint, Michigan, sit-down of 1936–37). The word became famous on February 1, 1960, when four Black students from North Carolina A&T sat at the whites-only lunch counter of the Woolworth’s in Greensboro and would not leave; within weeks sit-ins had spread across the South. Later in the decade students borrowed the form for campus and anti-war protest, and it spawned the teach-in, the love-in, and the be-in.
biblical_def: A sit-in is a protest in which demonstrators occupy a place — a lunch counter, a dean’s office, a lobby — and refuse to leave until their demand is heard. The Christian observation: the sit-in has a noble and a careless history, and Scripture helps a family tell them apart. Its noble beginning was the Greensboro lunch counter, where young men in jackets and ties sat quietly, endured abuse without striking back, and accepted arrest. That is a recognizable biblical shape: Daniel’s friends who said, "But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods" (Dan 3:18); Esther, who went to the king "which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish" (Est 4:16). The prophet’s demand stood behind it: "let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream" (Amo 5:24). But the same form, borrowed later for every grievance under the sun, often lost the humility that made it righteous. A sit-in that is disciplined, nonviolent, aimed at real injustice, and willing to bear the penalty can be the Christian’s plea to the conscience of the magistrate. A sit-in that is a tantrum with a manifesto is not. The rule of Micah fits every protest: "to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God" (Mic 6:8) — and the third clause is the one most often forgotten.
webster_summary: Boomer-era protest (Greensboro, February 1, 1960) in which demonstrators occupy a place and refuse to leave — righteous when it is humble, nonviolent, and willing to suffer for real justice (Mic 6:8; Est 4:16).
webster_full: SIT-IN, n. (1960; Boomer era) A form of protest in which demonstrators occupy a public place, especially one from which they have been excluded, and refuse to leave. "The Greensboro sit-in." Also v. to sit in.

Webster (1828) — SIT, verb intransitive preterit tense sat; old participle passive sitten [Latin sedeo.] 1. To rest upon the buttocks, as animals; as, to sit on a sofa or on the ground. 2. To perch; to rest on the feet; as fowls. 3. To occupy a seat or place in an official capacity. The scribes and the Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat. Matthew 23:2 . 4. To be in a state of rest or idleness. Shall your brethren go to war, and shall ye sit here? Numbers 32:6 .
Derivatives of the 1960s: teach-in (1965), love-in (1967), be-in (1967).
Decode for families: ask of any protest what Micah asks — is it just, is it merciful, is it humble?
scriptures: Mic 6:8
He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?
Amo 5:24
But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
Est 4:16

Go, gather together all the Jews that are present in Shushan, and fast ye for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day: I also and my maidens will fast likewise; and so will I go in unto the king, which is not according to the law: and if I perish, I perish.
Dan 3:18
But if not, be it known unto thee, O king, that we will not serve thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up.
Act 5:29
Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men.
corruption_summary: The sit-in began as humble, suffering witness against real injustice and drifted into a reflex for every grievance; Scripture keeps the first and judges the second by Micah’s threefold rule.
corruption_paragraphs: The Greensboro four did not shout, did not destroy, and did not hide their faces. They sat, they ordered coffee, they were refused, and they came back the next day with more friends. Much of the early civil-rights movement was organized from Black churches and sung in the language of the Psalms, and its discipline came from there. That is why it carried moral weight. It was not merely defiance; it was a plea to the conscience, made at personal cost, in the manner of Esther who went in to the king "which is not according to the law" and said, "if I perish, I perish" (Est 4:16).

By 1968 the form had been emptied out. Students sat in to demand anything and everything, and the cost was often borne by others — the janitors, the classmates, the taxpayers. A protest that seizes what it wants is no longer a plea; it is a raid. Scripture does not forbid the believer to refuse an unjust order (Act 5:29), but it binds the manner of the refusal as tightly as the reason for it. Justice, mercy, and humility walk together (Mic 6:8), or the protest becomes one more injustice in the name of justice.
roots_summary: Old English sittan + in; 1930s sit-down strike → February 1, 1960 Greensboro lunch-counter sit-in → 1960s campus and anti-war sit-ins.
roots_lines: Old English sittan — to sit, to be seated; to dwell; to occupy a place
1936–37: the Flint sit-down strike gives the labor movement the occupation protest
February 1, 1960: four North Carolina A&T students sit at the Greensboro Woolworth’s counter
1960s: sit-ins spread across the South, then to campuses and anti-war protest
Offspring: teach-in (1965), love-in and be-in (1967)
usage: "Granddad says he saw the Greensboro sit-in on the news and it changed his mind about a lot of things."
Do justly, love mercy, walk humbly (Mic 6:8) — the test of any protest.
Righteous refusal accepts the cost: "if I perish, I perish" (Est 4:16).

etymology: Formed in 1967 on the pattern of sit-in (1960) and teach-in (1965). The best-remembered love-in was held in Elysian Park, Los Angeles, on Easter Sunday 1967, followed by others in New York, San Francisco, and on college greens that summer: open-air gatherings with music, flowers, face paint, and the hope of universal brotherhood — and, frequently, drugs and casual sex.
biblical_def: A love-in was a hippie gathering of 1967 and after: thousands of young people in a park, music playing, flowers and incense, everyone embracing everyone, all of it meant as a living demonstration that love could replace hatred. The Christian observation: the hunger was real and the food was false. The young people of 1967 were hungry for a fellowship where strangers became family, where walls came down, where love was more than talk. Scripture describes exactly that — and locates it in the church of Jesus Christ: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another" (Joh 13:35). But the love-in tried to have the fellowship without the Lord, and so it ended up with the counterfeit. Love without truth curdles into sentiment, and love without holiness curdles into lust. Scripture defines the real thing from the top down: "Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins" (1Jn 4:10). Love begins in God’s gift, not in our feelings, and it is proved by deeds, not by a festival: "let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth" (1Jn 3:18). A grandparent who went to a love-in can be told: you were looking for the church and did not know it. Every Lord’s Day there is a gathering where strangers become brothers, and the love there was bought with blood.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (1967) for a hippie gathering celebrating universal love — a real hunger for fellowship that Scripture satisfies only in the church, where love begins in God’s gift of His Son (1Jn 4:10).
webster_full: LOVE-IN, n. (Boomer slang, 1967) A public gathering of hippies, typically in a park, for music, celebration, and the expression of universal love and peace; often accompanied by drug use. "The Easter love-in at Elysian Park."

Webster (1828) — LOVE, noun 1. An affection of the mind excited by beauty and worth of any kind, or by the qualities of an object which communicate pleasure, sensual or intellectual. It is opposed to hatred. love between the sexes, is a compound affection, consisting of esteem, benevolence, and animal desire. love is excited by pleasing qualities of any kind, as by kindness, benevolence, charity, and by the qualities which render social intercourse agreeable. In the latter case, love is ardent friendship, or a strong attachment springing from good will and esteem, and the pleasure derived from the company, civilities and kindness of others. Between certain natural relatives, love seems to be in some cases instinctive. Such is the love of a mother for her child, which manifests itself toward an infant, before any particular qualities in the child are unfolded.
Formed on sit-in and teach-in; compare be-in, happening.
Decode for families: the love-in promised the fellowship the church is commanded to be. Ask whether your congregation looks like Joh 13:35.
scriptures: By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
Herein is love, not that we loved God, but that he loved us, and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.
My little children, let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth.
Rom 12:9
Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good.
Gal 5:13
For, brethren, ye have been called unto liberty; only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but by love serve one another.
corruption_summary: The love-in sought brotherhood without the Father and love without holiness; Scripture defines love from God down (1Jn 4:10) and proves it in deed and in truth (1Jn 3:18).
corruption_paragraphs: The love-in turned love into an event. You went to it, felt it, and went home. That is the cardinal error of sentimental religion in every age: love becomes a mood that visits a crowd, rather than a covenant that binds a person. Paul’s command, "Let love be without dissimulation. Abhor that which is evil; cleave to that which is good" (Rom 12:9), joins love to moral judgment in a single breath. The love-in separated them. It had no abhorring and no cleaving — only embracing — and so it could not tell a brother from a predator, and the predators came.

Scripture does not answer the love-in by being cold. It answers by being specific. Love is the Father sending the Son (1Jn 4:10). Love is the Son washing feet. Love is bearing a brother’s burden on a Tuesday when no one is singing. "By love serve one another" (Gal 5:13) is less photogenic than a crowd in Elysian Park, and it is the only kind that lasts until the next Easter.
roots_summary: Old English lufu + in, on the pattern of sit-in (1960) / teach-in (1965) → love-in, Easter 1967, Los Angeles.
roots_lines: Old English lufu — love, affection, desire
Greek agapē — the self-giving love of God (1Jn 4:10) and of the brethren (Joh 13:35)
1960 sit-in, 1965 teach-in → the -in suffix for any mass gathering
Easter Sunday 1967: love-in at Elysian Park, Los Angeles
Summer 1967: love-ins in New York, San Francisco, and on campuses
usage: "Grandma went to one love-in, got a sunburn and a headache, and went back to church."
By this shall all men know (Joh 13:35) — the church is the gathering the love-in was looking for.
Love in deed and in truth (1Jn 3:18), not in a field and a feeling.

etymology: From the Human Be-In, a gathering of some 20,000–30,000 young people in the Polo Fields of Golden Gate Park, San Francisco, on January 14, 1967, billed as "A Gathering of the Tribes." Allen Ginsberg chanted, Timothy Leary first urged the crowd to "turn on, tune in, drop out," and the Grateful Dead and Jefferson Airplane played. The word, formed on sit-in, announced that the point was not to protest anything but simply to be — together, high, and present. It is generally reckoned the prelude to the Summer of Love.
biblical_def: A be-in was a gathering whose only purpose was being: no demands, no speeches with an agenda, just thousands of young people in a park existing together, often under the influence of LSD and Eastern mysticism. The Christian observation: the word reaches for something only God possesses. There is One whose name is simply Being. When Moses asked His name, "God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM" (Exo 3:14). Man does not have being in himself; he receives it moment by moment. Paul told the philosophers of Athens, quoting their own poets, "in him we live, and move, and have our being" (Act 17:28), and "by him all things consist" (Col 1:17). The be-in tried to find the ground of being by emptying the mind and filling the park, and it found instead the "turn on, tune in, drop out" of Leary — a drugged stillness. Scripture offers a different stillness: "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psa 46:10). That stillness is not a void but a Presence; it is not drugged but awake; and it does not dissolve the self into the crowd but brings the self before its Maker. The Lord Jesus took the divine name for Himself — "Before Abraham was, I am" — and a grandparent who stood in Golden Gate Park in 1967 looking for Being can be told where Being has a face.
webster_summary: Boomer slang from the Human Be-In (San Francisco, January 14, 1967) for a gathering whose purpose was simply to be — a reach toward the One whose name is I AM (Exo 3:14), in whom we have our being (Act 17:28).
webster_full: BE-IN, n. (Boomer slang, 1967) A large, unstructured gathering of hippies for no stated purpose but communal presence, music, and often drug use; from the Human Be-In, Golden Gate Park, January 14, 1967.
Formed on sit-in (1960); compare love-in (1967), happening (1959).
Decode for families: the be-in was a mystical event — Eastern chant, LSD, and the hope of cosmic oneness. Its descendants are the festival and the "vibe."
scriptures: Exo 3:14
And God said unto Moses, I AM THAT I AM: and he said, Thus shalt thou say unto the children of Israel, I AM hath sent me unto you.
For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring.
Col 1:17
And he is before all things, and by him all things consist.
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth.
corruption_summary: The be-in sought the ground of being by drugs, crowds, and the emptied mind; Scripture names the ground of being as I AM THAT I AM, known not by dissolving the self but by bowing it.
corruption_paragraphs: The be-in was more religious than political. Ginsberg led Hindu chants from the stage; the posters drew on astrology and Eastern iconography; the drug was taken as a sacrament. The young were rejecting the thin, Sunday-only Christianity many of them had been raised in, and reaching instead for an experience of the infinite. Scripture would say they were right that the infinite exists and wrong about how it is met. Paul’s Athens sermon fits the be-in exactly: you are very religious; you worship what you do not know; let me declare Him to you — the God "in him we live, and move, and have our being" (Act 17:28).

The mystical road teaches that God is found by losing the distinction between yourself and everything else. The biblical road teaches the opposite: God is found when that distinction is most sharply felt — the creature before the Creator, the sinner before the Holy One, Isaiah crying "Woe is me." "Be still, and know that I am God" (Psa 46:10) is not an invitation to dissolve; it is a command to stop and acknowledge who is God and who is not. Only then does the gospel come, and the One who said "I am" says also, "Come unto me."
roots_summary: Old English beon (to be) + in, on the pattern of sit-in → the Human Be-In, Golden Gate Park, January 14, 1967.
roots_lines: Old English beon — to be, to exist
Hebrew ehyeh asher ehyeh — "I AM THAT I AM" (Exo 3:14), the self-existent God
1960 sit-in → 1960s -in gatherings
January 14, 1967: the Human Be-In, "A Gathering of the Tribes," San Francisco
Spring–summer 1967: be-ins in New York’s Central Park and elsewhere
usage: "Your great-uncle was at the Human Be-In. He says he doesn’t remember much, which tells you something."
In him we live, and move, and have our being (Act 17:28).
Be still, and know that I am God (Psa 46:10) — stillness before a Person, not a void.

etymology: From happen (Middle English hap, chance, from Old Norse happ, luck). As a noun for a staged, partly improvised art event it was coined by the artist Allan Kaprow, whose 18 Happenings in 6 Parts was performed at the Reuben Gallery, New York, in October 1959. By the mid-1960s a happening was any spontaneous party or event, and by 1967 the adjective happening ("this place is happening") meant lively, fashionable, where the action is. The Supremes’ "The Happening" reached No. 1 in 1967.
biblical_def: In Boomer slang a happening was a spontaneous event — part art show, part party, part street theater — and a happening place was wherever the excitement was. To be where it was happening was the whole goal. The Christian observation: the word is built on hap, chance, and it carries a whole philosophy inside it — that life is a series of unplanned moments and the best thing is to be present for the exciting ones. Scripture has two answers. The first concerns chance. Nothing merely happens. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33). What looks like a happening is providence, and for God’s people it is a good providence: "all things work together for good to them that love God" (Rom 8:28). The second concerns the hunger for novelty. Luke records that the Athenians "spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell, or to hear some new thing" (Act 17:21), and the Preacher had already said, "there is no new thing under the sun" (Ecc 1:9). The restless search for where it is happening is a symptom of a heart that has not found rest. Augustine said it plainly: our heart is restless until it rests in Thee. The truly happening place in any town is the Lord’s Table, where the greatest event in history is shown forth until He come.
webster_summary: Boomer slang (from Allan Kaprow’s 1959 art events) for a spontaneous event, and as an adjective for a lively, fashionable place — built on hap (chance), which Scripture replaces with providence (Pro 16:33).
webster_full: HAPPENING, n. (1959; Boomer slang) A spontaneous or loosely staged event combining art, theater, and audience participation; hence any lively, unplanned gathering. "There’s a happening at the gallery tonight."
HAPPENING, adj. (Boomer slang, later 1960s; revived in later decades) Fashionable, exciting, full of activity. "This club is happening." "What’s happening?" — a greeting.

Webster (1828) — HAPPEN, verb intransitive hap’n. 1. To come by chance; to come without one’s previous expectation; to fall out. There shall no evil happen to the just. Proverbs 12:21 . 2. To come; to befall. They talked together of all those things which had happened. Luke 24:14 . 3. To light; to fall or come unexpectedly. I have happened on some other accounts relating to mortalities.
Decode for families: where it’s happening is the ancestor of FOMO. Teach your children Pro 16:33 — nothing merely happens.
scriptures: The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD.
Rom 8:28
And we know that all things work together for good to them that love God, to them who are the called according to his purpose.
Ecc 1:9
The thing that hath been, it is that which shall be; and that which is done is that which shall be done: and there is no new thing under the sun.
(For all the Athenians and strangers which were there spent their time in nothing else, but either to tell, or to hear some new thing.)
corruption_summary: The happening celebrated chance and chased novelty; Scripture denies that anything merely happens and diagnoses the chase for the new as a restless heart.
corruption_paragraphs: Hap is an old word for luck, and happen once meant simply "to come by chance." The Boomer happening made a virtue of that: no script, no plan, no meaning beyond the moment. It was the artistic face of a worldview in which the universe is an accident and the best you can do is be present when something interesting occurs. The Christian cannot live in that universe. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33) — even the dice are governed. The believer does not chase happenings; he watches providence.

The adjective carried the same restlessness into everyday life. To be happening was to be where the action was, and the fear of missing it drove a generation from club to club and cause to cause. The Athenians of Act 17:21 lived the same way, and the Preacher had already priced it: "there is no new thing under the sun" (Ecc 1:9). The Christian is not bored; he is at rest. The most important thing that ever happened has already happened, outside Jerusalem, on a hill, and every Lord’s Day he is where that is shown forth.
roots_summary: Old Norse happ (luck) → Middle English hap, happen (to come by chance) → 1959 Kaprow’s Happenings → 1960s slang noun and adjective.
roots_lines: Old Norse happ — chance, good luck → Middle English hap
Middle English happenen — to come to pass, especially by chance
October 1959: Allan Kaprow, 18 Happenings in 6 Parts, Reuben Gallery, New York
Mid-1960s: happening — any spontaneous party or event; 1967 "The Happening" (the Supremes)
Late 1960s onward: adj. happening, lively, fashionable; "What’s happening?"
usage: "Grandpa asked if the youth group was ‘happening.’ We said yes to be nice."
Nothing merely happens: the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD (Pro 16:33).
There is no new thing under the sun (Ecc 1:9) — and the One who made the sun is never stale.

etymology: The name given to the summer of 1967, when as many as 100,000 young people converged on the Haight-Ashbury district of San Francisco, drawn by the Human Be-In (January), the Monterey Pop Festival (June), Scott McKenzie’s hit "San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)" (May), and national press coverage of the hippie scene. Local organizers formed a "Council for the Summer of Love" in the spring; by October the Diggers staged a mock "Death of Hippie" funeral to mark its end.
biblical_def: The Summer of Love is shorthand for 1967 in San Francisco: flowers in the hair, free concerts in the park, free food from the Diggers, LSD, communal crash pads, and the conviction that a new age of peace and freedom was dawning. Many grandparents remember it as the high-water mark of their youth. The Christian observation: it promised liberty and delivered bondage within a single season. Peter saw it nineteen centuries early: "While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption" (2Pe 2:19). By autumn the Haight was a slum of hard drugs, venereal disease, runaways, and predators; the Diggers held a funeral for the hippie in October. It was the law of the harvest working on schedule: "whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap" (Gal 6:7). And Jeremiah’s lament could have been written on a Haight Street wall that fall: "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved" (Jer 8:20). Yet God did not abandon those children. Within three years, out of the same streets, the Jesus Movement was baptizing hippies in the Pacific by the thousands. The summer of love ended; the love of God did not. "The world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever" (1Jn 2:17).
webster_summary: The name for 1967 in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury, when some 100,000 young people sought peace and free love — a promise of liberty that became bondage by autumn (2Pe 2:19), and a harvest that ended unsaved (Jer 8:20).
webster_full: SUMMER OF LOVE, n. (proper; 1967) The summer of 1967, when tens of thousands of young people gathered in San Francisco’s Haight-Ashbury and elsewhere to celebrate the hippie counterculture of peace, free love, music, and drugs; used generally for the high point of 1960s idealism.

Webster (1828) — SUMMER, noun With us, the season of the year comprehended in the months June, July and August; during which time, the sun being north of the equator, shines more directly upon this part of the earth, which, together with the increased length of the days, renders this the hottest period of the year. In latitudes south of the equator, just the opposite takes place, or it is summer there when it is winter here. The entire year is also sometimes divided into summer and winter, the former signifying the warmer and the latter the colder part of the year.
Decode for families: the Summer of Love was followed by the fall of the Haight. Ask a grandparent what came after September.
scriptures: While they promise them liberty, they themselves are the servants of corruption: for of whom a man is overcome, of the same is he brought in bondage.
Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Gal 6:8
For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.
Jer 8:20
The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved.
And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
corruption_summary: The Summer of Love promised a new age of liberty and love and harvested addiction and exploitation by autumn; Scripture calls that the promise of liberty from servants of corruption (2Pe 2:19).
corruption_paragraphs: The romance of 1967 survives because it is remembered by the survivors. The runaways who never went home, the girls exploited in the crash pads, the young men burned out on speed and heroin by Christmas — they do not write the anniversary retrospectives. The Diggers themselves, who had fed the crowds all summer, carried a coffin down Haight Street in October 1967 marked "Hippie, Son of Media." The movement knew it had been sold something. Paul names the transaction: "he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption" (Gal 6:8).

The Christian telling of 1967 must not end there, because God’s story did not. The same young people who went west looking for love were met, a few years later, by the Jesus People — long-haired evangelists in the same streets with Bibles instead of tabs. Many of the Boomer generation’s pastors and missionaries came out of that wreckage. The summer ended; the harvest that saves did not. "He that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting" (Gal 6:8).
roots_summary: Old English sumor + love; spring 1967 "Council for the Summer of Love," San Francisco → the name for the whole 1967 hippie season.
roots_lines: Old English sumor — summer, the warm season; in Scripture the season of harvest (Jer 8:20)
January 1967: the Human Be-In; May 1967: "San Francisco (Be Sure to Wear Flowers in Your Hair)"
June 1967: the Monterey Pop Festival
Summer 1967: up to 100,000 young people in Haight-Ashbury
October 6, 1967: the Diggers’ "Death of Hippie" mock funeral
usage: "Grandpa went to San Francisco for the Summer of Love and came home in August with a cough and no money."
They promise liberty, but are servants of corruption (2Pe 2:19).
The harvest is past, the summer is ended (Jer 8:20) — but the call of the gospel is still today.

etymology: From the Youth International Party, founded on New Year’s Eve 1967 by Abbie Hoffman, Jerry Rubin, Paul Krassner, and others; the name was built backward from the shout yippee! and played on hippie. The Yippies were a theatrical radical group, best known for disrupting the 1968 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, where they nominated a pig named "Pigasus" for president, and for throwing dollar bills onto the floor of the New York Stock Exchange in 1967.
biblical_def: A Yippie was a member of the Youth International Party, the prankster wing of the 1960s radical left: hippies turned political, who used mockery, street theater, and stunts to humiliate authority. Their most famous act was nominating a pig for president at the 1968 Democratic Convention. The Christian observation: Yippie politics was the politics of the scoffer, and Scripture has a great deal to say about him. The first Psalm blesses the man who does not sit "in the seat of the scornful" (Psa 1:1). Proverbs describes the prankster who does real damage and then laughs it off: "As a mad man who casteth firebrands, arrows, and death, So is the man that deceiveth his neighbour, and saith, Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:18–19). The Yippies discovered that mockery is a powerful weapon in a television age, and every movement since has borrowed it. But mockery can only tear down; it cannot build or heal. "Fools make a mock at sin" (Pro 14:9), and a culture trained to laugh at every authority eventually laughs at the moral law itself. Peter warned that "there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts" (2Pe 3:3). Satire has a place — Elijah mocked the prophets of Baal — but Elijah mocked idols in the name of the living God. The Yippies mocked everything in the name of nothing, and their grandchildren have inherited the sneer without the cause.
webster_summary: Boomer slang for a member of the Youth International Party (founded December 31, 1967), the prankster radicals of the 1968 Chicago convention — the politics of the scoffer Scripture warns against (Psa 1:1; Pro 26:19).
webster_full: YIPPIE, n. (Boomer slang, 1968) A member of the Youth International Party, a radical, theatrical, anti-establishment group founded December 31, 1967; hence any politically radical hippie given to pranks and street theater.
From Y.I.P. (Youth International Party) + yippee (a shout of joy) + hippie.
Decode for families: Yippie tactics — humiliate, provoke, film it — are the ancestor of the political meme and the viral stunt.

corruption_summary: The Yippies made mockery a political method and every authority a target; Scripture blesses the man who will not sit in the seat of the scornful and warns of scoffers walking after their own lusts.
corruption_paragraphs: The Yippie insight was that ridicule disarms authority faster than argument. A pig nominated for president, money rained on stockbrokers, a plan announced to levitate the Pentagon — each stunt made the powerful look foolish on the evening news, and the cameras did the rest. It worked, and the method outlived the movement. But Scripture distrusts the scorner precisely because scorn is so effective and so cheap. It asks nothing of the mocker but a camera and an audience, and it trains him to treat seriousness itself as the enemy. "Fools make a mock at sin" (Pro 14:9).

The biblical model of holy mockery is Elijah on Carmel, and the contrast is instructive. Elijah mocked a false god in the name of the true God, at the risk of his life, and then called down fire to prove it. The Yippie mocked a flawed order in the name of no order at all, at no risk to himself, and then went to the party. Proverbs calls that the madman with firebrands who says, "Am not I in sport?" (Pro 26:19). A father can teach his son the difference: laugh at idols, never at holiness, and never as a substitute for doing something better.
roots_summary: Acronym Y.I.P. (Youth International Party, December 31, 1967) + yippee! + hippie → Yippie; 1968 Chicago DNC, "Pigasus."
roots_lines: Yippee — American shout of joy, early 20th c.
Hippie — 1960s counterculture youth (see Hippie)
December 31, 1967: Youth International Party founded (Hoffman, Rubin, Krassner)
August 1968: Yippies at the Chicago Democratic National Convention; the pig "Pigasus" nominated
Scripture: the scorner and the scoffer (Psa 1:1; Pro 14:9; 2Pe 3:3)
usage: "Your great-uncle wasn’t a hippie, he was a Yippie — he says there’s a difference. Grandma says the difference was more arrests."
Blessed is the man that sitteth not in the seat of the scornful (Psa 1:1).
Mock idols if you must; never mock holiness, and never mistake a sneer for a solution.
